#33552. Industry News: Karl Bushby Reaches Mother's House, Ending 28-Year Journey Around the World

📅 02 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3368 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Karl Bushby Reaches Mother's House, Ending 28-Year Journey Around the World

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3368 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, “This is absolute madness,” mentioned a happy Karl Bushby, as hundreds of people welcomed him home in a civic ceremony in his hometown of Hull, England.
  • The reunion with his mother a couple of hours later was equally public, as the pair were surrounded by TV cameras and hundreds of well-wishers.
  • When Karl Bushby quietly set off from the southern tip of South America on November 1 of that year, it was very different.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, “This is absolute madness,” mentioned a happy Karl Bushby, as hundreds of people welcomed him home in a civic ceremony in his hometown of Hull, England. In a scene that couldn’t be more different from the past 28 years that he has spent walking around the world, Bushby stood underneath a giant Welcome Home Karl sign, made an appreciative speech, then begged off to continue walking the final few steps to his mother’s house, which he left back in 1998.

The reunion with his mother a couple of hours later was equally public, as the pair were surrounded by TV cameras and hundreds of well-wishers.

When Karl Bushby quietly set off from the southern tip of South America on November 1 of that year, it was very different. Bushby was 29 years old. He is now 57. When he began, he had around $500 in his pocket, a two-wheeled cart loaded with supplies, and an idea that most people would have dismissed as a fantasy. He was going to walk home to Hull, England, without using any transport. He would not return to the UK until he could do so on foot. He expected the expedition to take about 12 years. Instead, it has taken 28.

According to recent reports, bushby has spent more than 10,000 days and 50,000km pursuing that single objective. The Goliath Expedition has become one of the longest and most unusual human-powered adventures in modern exploration, and he is nervous about it ending. Speaking to The Washington Post as he approached home, he mentioned: “My purpose and reason for living is about to end. It’s going to be difficult…trying to blend back into a society that you just don’t know anymore.”.

Through Chile’s Atacama Desert. Photo: Karl Bushby.

While serving with the Parachute Regiment, Bushby received a birthday card from his father, Keith, who had served in the British Army. In it was a story about special forces soldiers debating whether it was possible to walk from London to New York via the Bering Strait. Looking at a world map, Bushby began tracing the route himself.

But rather than stopping at Fresh York, he extended the line south through the Americas, all the way to the tip of Chile. The result was an expedition that would take him from the southernmost reaches of South America back to his home in England.

Sources indicate that “That was the moment the hairs on the back of your neck stand up,” he told GQ Magazine. “You think, well, that’s it.” He did some calculations, created a timeline on the “back of a beer mat,” and estimated the journey would take him 12 years. From that point, Bushby showed nothing but determination. At the start, most people doubted it was even possible. That only made him more certain that he wanted to try.

Industry observers note that he gave himself two rules. The first was that he could not use any transportation, even self-propelled vehicles like bicycles or kayaks, to advance the expedition. The second was that he could not return to the UK until he had completed the walk. Those rules sound simple. In practice, they created multiple logistical nightmares and affected almost every aspect of his life.

2001, the Darien Gap. Photo: Karl Bushby.

According to recent reports, bushby left Punta Arenas, Chile, with his equipment loaded onto a cart he calls The Beast. He was not an elite endurance athlete embarking on a carefully funded and organized expedition. He was a young former paratrooper with a few hundred dollars, a rough line on a map, and limited resources. He had no supporters or funding, and relied on gas station food or what locals gave him.

“The first years, you’re living the boys’ adventure dream, and it’s great,” he told The New York Times, “and then it really becomes a grind.”.

In a recent development, the first few years took him north through the Americas, including multiple conflict zones. In Peru, he was attacked by a mob; in Colombia, he floated down the crocodile-laden Atrato River to avoid being spotted by armed men. Then he faced the Darien Gap, that infamously dangerous stretch between Colombia and Panama, ruled by drug and human smugglers, that almost all adventurers skirt around.

Recent findings suggest that eventually, he reached Panama. But emerging from the jungle did not mean he was free to continue. After crossing a restricted border zone without the necessary visa, he was detained for 18 days.

Industry observers note that after making his way through the Americas, Bushby eventually finished crossing the U.S., where he had picked up a few sponsorships, and reached Alaska. The next major obstacle, and the one that catapulted his journey into world news, was the Bering Strait, the stretch of water separating North America from Russia.

North America. Photo: Karl Bushby.

The Arctic had already given Bushby a taste of its dangers. During the Alaskan stage of the expedition, he was rescued by helicopter after becoming stranded on an ice floe that broke away from the coast and drifted out to sea, and had a standoff with a polar bear. He knew how risky the Bering Strait crossing would be.

Recent findings suggest that in March 2006, Bushby and French adventurer Dimitri Kieffer spent 14 days crossing the Bering Strait between Alaska and Russia on foot. With 90kg sleds, they traveled across the shifting ice in temperatures that fell to around -30˚C, against the prevailing winds as the ice moved beneath them.

Wearing dry suits, they had to swim at points through the icy, slushy water. “All night long, you’re just listening to the grinding, and the ice is just like screaming,” he told The Newly introduced York Times. “We actually had to evacuate the tent during the night because the thing started to break apart beneath us.”.

Industry observers note that they made it across, achieving a rare crossing of one of the world’s most formidable natural barriers. But reaching Russia did not mean the difficulties were over. Russian authorities detained the pair for entering the country without the required permission. They faced the possibility of deportation.

Recent findings suggest that crossing the Bering Strait. Photo: Karl Bushby.

Industry observers note that russia would consume years of Bushby’s life. He had to leave the country every 90 days because his tourist visa allowed him to stay in Russia for only 90 of every 180 days. Then in 2008, his journey came to a standstill. He lost sponsorship and could not travel to Russia for a few years. In 2011, he resumed his trek, again in 90-day stints. Then in 2012, he was denied a further visa, and in 2013, he received a five-year entry ban from Russia.

Here, Bushby responded with an extraordinary protest. He walked approximately 5,000km from Los Angeles to the Russian Embassy in Washington, D.C., hoping to draw attention to his predicament and secure the paperwork he needed to continue.

The years of delay exposed another unusual aspect of the expedition. Bushby’s rules did not mean he had to remain indefinitely in the country where he was stuck. Nor did they prevent him from using transport for journeys unrelated to advancing his route home. However, he couldn’t fly back to the UK during these hiatuses.

Sources indicate that when visas, funding, or political restrictions prevented him from continuing, he could fly elsewhere, take a break, and wait until circumstances allowed him to resume. But he could not use that flight to skip a section of the route. Whenever he returned, he had to pick up from the exact point where he had stopped. Most of the time, he decamped to Mexico. Its lower cost of living made it a practical place to wait. He also spent time in the United States.

Bushby and Dimitri Kieffer, 2006. Photo: Karl Bushby.

Recent findings suggest that the distinction mattered enormously to the expedition. Bushby could board a plane to escape a logistical dead end, but when he returned to the route, he had to pick up where he had stopped. He could not simply fly over the awkward section and resume walking on the other side.

It has been revealed that the arrangement might seem to stretch the definition of walking around the world. But for Bushby, it was the only way to maintain his two original rules without spending years of his life waiting at a closed border. Some visa delays took years to resolve. And the longer the journey continued, the harder it became to predict when, or even whether, it would end. Getting across Russia alone took almost 10 years.

Sources indicate that he lived cheaply but still needed money to survive on this near-endless journey. Some of it came from the sponsorships he eventually acquired. During what sounded like a particularly low point 15 years ago, on one of his hiatuses in Mexico while trying to overcome another logistical hurdle on his journey, he told Backpacker magazine:.

Sources indicate that I’m 42 years old and I’m broke and I’m homeless. I’m a professional parasite. I’m a professional hobo. I’m sleeping on other people’s couches. I’m 42 years old, and I have to walk other people’s dogs, just so they’ll feed me. My job is picking up dog shit!

According to recent reports, the passage of time is one of the most striking aspects of Bushby’s story. His expedition began in an era before smartphones, Instagram, and the expectation of sharing every stage of an adventure online. The young man who left Chile in 1998 could never have imagined that nearly three decades later, people around the world would be following his progress toward his childhood home. The fact that so many people are following it still baffles Bushby.

According to recent reports, while Bushby was away, life continued for the people he had left behind. His son, Adam, grew up, and his family had to get on with their lives without him. Adam was eight when he set off. He is now 36, with a family of his own, including a 12-year-old daughter whom Bushby has never met.

When his dad started the walk, Adam didn’t fully understand what was going on, or know how to explain it to people who asked. Over the years, they have tried to stay in touch and maintain some kind of relationship. At 14, Adam flew to Alaska to see his dad. It was six years after the expedition began and a turning point for him in accepting what Bushby was doing. “I did feel a bit awkward because at that point I didn’t really know my dad,” he told GQ Magazine.

In a recent development, they later spent 10 days walking together as part of a National Geographic documentary project. Adam described the experience as surreal, suddenly stepping into his father’s world. They have spoken regularly since, but as Adam put it: “[His] life went this way, and I went that way, two separate routes.”.

Sources indicate that in various interviews, Adam has explained that he had nothing against his father’s ambition, that he respects what he has done and is very proud of him. But also that growing up without him had been difficult.

Sources indicate that karl Bushby has not seen other members of his family for years. He met Adam when he stepped out of the water after crossing the English Channel back to England, but he has not seen his mother in over a decade, even though he will be living with her once he arrives back at his childhood home. He recognizes how difficult the situation will be and that it is due to his choices over the last 30 years.

“The relationship between me and my son is good, but there’s a lot to resolve there,” he told GQ Magazine. “I’ve got a granddaughter I’ve never seen, and then dear old mother, Lord. I have to live with my mother now. I’m going from a global adventure to living with my mother in a basement at 57. This is going to be a challenge.”.

Life on the road has often been lonely, but Bushby has seen kindness and hospitality in every corner of the globe. “I’ve been welcomed in by the poorest of the poor,” he told The Washington Post. “I’ve met 99.9999% of the very best of humanity. Every culture, every country, has been the same response.”.

Recent findings suggest that he has also had two significant romantic relationships during the expedition. He spent around seven years with a Colombian woman. Later, he had a three-year relationship with a woman from Japan. He met both while on the expedition, and it was also the reason both broke down.

After finally getting across Russia, Bushby continued through Mongolia, where he joined with other adventurers, including Angela Maxwell, to trek across the Gobi Desert with camels. After 1,130km and several disagreements, the group went their separate ways, and Busby continued into China by himself. In 2018, he crossed Kazakhstan and then made his way through Uzbekistan and Turkmenistan. Once again, visa issues ground the journey to a standstill. He could not get into Iran.

At the same time, the world was struck down by the pandemic. More years of waiting in Mexico began, even though Bushby still had a substantial distance to cover. Eventually, in 2022, he was on the move again. Once again joined by Angela Maxwell, he did something he had never intended doing during the expedition — swimming across the Caspian Sea.

Visa challenges and geopolitics meant he was unable to cross into Iran. So he came up with a fresh plan. He and Maxwell went back to Uzbekistan and took a different route. They walked across the Kyzylkum Desert until they reached the Caspian Sea. A self-proclaimed terrible swimmer, he was completely outside of his comfort zone. Wearing a wetsuit and flotation equipment, he described his floating-and-swimming hybrid as floatimming. It might not have been the most elegant crossing, but after 32 days at sea, 27 of which he was swimming with Maxwell and two Azerbaijani swimmers in very choppy waters, he completed the 288km swim.

In a recent development, back on solid ground, his next job was to get across Azerbaijan and into Turkey. Here, he hit a huge milestone. He crossed the Bosphorus Bridge on May 2, 2025. This meant he was back in Europe for the first time since he started walking.

In a recent development, the remaining distance to Britain was comparatively short, but the final stages were not straightforward. Once again, visa restrictions were the thorn in his side. Limited to traveling for 90 days at a time before having to leave Europe, he continued to use Mexico as a base as he waited for his 90 days to reset and tackled the remaining distance in short stretches.

Industry observers note that he made it through Turkey, Bulgaria, and Romania before confronting the next problem. Bushby always knew one of the logistical challenges would be getting from France to England. He started trying to pull a plan together. Unsurprisingly, for someone who has walked across the world, his goal was to cross it via the Channel Tunnel. The issue was that this was forbidden. He had hoped to use their service tunnel, but his request was denied.

According to recent reports, karl Bushby speaks at a civic ceremony in Hull, England earlier today. Photo: YouTube.

As he continued walking through Hungary and Austria, he attempted to appeal the decision, reaching out to anyone who might help, to no avail. “We have carefully considered his request and explored a range of possible options. In this instance, regretfully, we are unable to accommodate Mr Bushby’s wishes,” a spokesperson for the Eurotunnel told the BBC. This meant the only alternative was to get back into the water and swim the Channel.

Still walking, he had made it to Germany. Then he picked his way across Belgium and France, all the while decamping to Mexico, Canada, or the U.S. every 90 days, and trying to piece together a plan for swimming the Channel. This proved to be another headache regarding permissions.

Recent findings suggest that french rules stop anyone swimming the Channel from France to Britain. He thought he had been granted an exemption, but in September, he learned that was not the case. After much negotiation, he finally got the go-ahead. On October 5, Bushby finally landed back on British soil at Shakespeare Beach near Dover after swimming the English Channel.

The crossing took three days. He spent around 20 hours in the water, spent the nights on a safety vessel, and dropped back into the water at his last-known position each morning.

Sources indicate that after 28 years abroad, he was finally back in the country he had left in 1998. But rather than feeling joy, he told The Newly introduced York Times he felt a real sense of loss. After three decades on the road, the prospect of just 400km to go was hugely daunting. “I’m about to lose my purpose for living,” he remarked. “It’s about to abruptly end.”.

In a recent development, he is nervous about what comes next and reintegrating into a society he no longer knows. He is considering retraining as a teacher, as he loved giving talks in schools as he walked.

According to recent reports, one significant question is why Bushby has become so celebrated. He is not the first person to have attempted a long-distance walk around the world. Other adventurers have spent years traveling between countries, crossing continents on foot, or undertaking journeys without motorized transport, but Bushby has singularly captured the world’s attention.

In a recent development, karl Bushby, back turned, leaves the civic ceremony to walk the last few steps to his mother’s house. Photo: YouTube.

Sources indicate that it might be the particular combination of his rules, or the fact that his objective is immediately understandable. He left home, and he is walking back. There is no complicated scientific mission to explain, no specialized equipment that the public needs to understand, and no obscure record category he is aiming for. The simplicity of it gives the story an almost fable-like quality, even though the journey was not simple at all.

It has been revealed that with just two rules, the expedition is relatively easy to follow. Every delay matters because Bushby cannot simply skip ahead. He is forced to wait or find another solution when something blocks his route. The question becomes how he will get around it without abandoning his principles.

It has been revealed that then there is the sheer amount of time it has taken. People who first encountered Bushby’s expedition in their twenties are now well into middle age themselves. Initially, there were no updates on social media. Instead, there was the odd news article that cropped up every few years about the same man, still walking across the world. A story that seemed like an ambitious adventure morphed into an entire adult life on the road.

Bushby has not necessarily made the journey look enjoyable. His progress has depended as much, if not more, on navigating bureaucracy and finding support as on putting one foot in front of the other. Despite it all, he continued.

As the journey has hit an era where we can follow an adventurer’s progress in real time, every obstacle and milestone has renewed interest in the question that has followed Bushby for 28 years: Will he actually make it home?

Now that he has to confront a latest question: How do you cope with coming home after three decades? “I will have to figure out who I am again. What is the meaning to it all? How do I find that meaning and purpose? How do I fill that hole I’m suddenly going to find myself in?” he told the BBC in the days before the expected end of the expedition. “I think the old adage goes…the only thing worse than a man who can’t fulfill his dreams is a man who’s fulfilled his dreams…because then what?”.

Everest and Ama Dablam Climbs Resume Despite Cyclone

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (583 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The second cyclone to hit Nepal’s mountains this season caused heavy snowfall last weekend, but its briefer stay has affected climbers and trekkers less.
  • It has been revealed that no cyclone seems enough to deter the Russian team on Everest for very long.
  • According to recent reports, the climbers’ latest foray up Everest’s West Ridge route.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The second cyclone to hit Nepal’s mountains this season caused heavy snowfall last weekend, but its briefer stay has affected climbers and trekkers less. As the sun returned this afternoon, fresh snow hampered smaller teams on 6,000m and 7,000m peaks, but the highly supported expeditions on Ama Dablam are proceeding with barely a hitch.

It has been revealed that no cyclone seems enough to deter the Russian team on Everest for very long. Leader Andrei Vasiliev told us yesterday from Kathmandu that he, Sergey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov will return to the mountain in one or two days. The trio is well aware of the challenge they face on Everest’s West Ridge, completely alone and without oxygen.

According to recent reports, the climbers’ latest foray up Everest’s West Ridge route. Photo: Andrei Vasiliev.

Vasiliev mentioned he is under some pressure due to unidentified “unsolved matters” but still determined to tackle the climb. In his own words:.

We know what needs to be done; the path is clear, and we must attempt to follow it. We’ve fallen ill. A massive amount of snow has fallen. You adapt promptly to upcoming conditions. Once we’re back in the snow, the cold, and the cramped tent, it will feel as though things were never any other way.

The new snow dump has thwarted some teams attempting Baruntse (7,129m) in the Khumbu. Jan McManus of Ireland was among them, and he has called off his expedition after failing to reach Camp 1 due to deep snow:.

It is unclear whether other climbers on the peak may still be trying. There were six large teams totaling 65 foreign climbers with permits for Baruntse.

Recent findings suggest that on Himlung (7,126m), teams hurried to summit and get down and safely away before the cyclone hit. During the previous snowstorm at the end of September, a massive avalanche buried Base Camp, killing 16 staff members. Despite the tragedy, one of the deadliest in Nepal’s mountaineering history, the peak remained open, and guided teams came in large numbers to the mountain a couple of weeks after the accident. A total of 130 foreigners had permits. Teams summited on October 25 and 26, and then left the area.

According to recent reports, ama Dablam Base Camp is also covered in snow, but the commercial teams will nevertheless resume climbing soon. According to Jana Schneider of Germany, climbing with 14 Peaks Expeditions, a Sherpa team is on its way to reopen those sections where fresh snow has buried the ropes. “If all goes well, my summit push begins Nov 4 until Nov 6,” she wrote.

It has been revealed that so far, 410 foreigners have applied for a permit to climb Ama Dablam. A Sherpa team first fixed the route on October 17, and dozens have summited since then. Despite the break forced by bad weather over the weekend, summits should continue throughout November.

One climber has perished on the mountain so far, and there have been some close calls. Paul Clarke of Australia and Xenia Santha of Hungary climbed Ama Dablam after attempting Dhaulagiri earlier this season. Their summit push was delayed as they found a 25-year-old climber in a serious situation at Camp 2. Santha and Clarke, who climbed without Sherpa support, gave the climber dexamethasone, spent the night with him, and helped organize an emergency airlift for the following morning. They continued to the summit one day later.

A high camp on Ama Dablam. Photo: Xenia Shanta.

Industry News: TA Tales: Phase 4 – The Comeback

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This post is dedicated to my dear friend Ionatana.
  • Industry observers note that after completing the Auckland section of Te Araroa, Maya and I, headed to Hamilton.
  • So, our recovery continued along the Waikato River.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This post is dedicated to my dear friend Ionatana. May God’s love, compassion, and mercy fill you, and your family up, then spill over with blessings.

Industry observers note that after completing the Auckland section of Te Araroa, Maya and I, headed to Hamilton. With a week of successful walking down, we felt another week of slack packing is maybe overly cautious, but (in my opinion) necessary. You can never be too careful when walking long distances. Taking care of injuries early, and not rushing through the recovery, is essential.

So, our recovery continued along the Waikato River. This is an established walkway for walkers, bikers, and boat racing watchers. Luckily for us, we managed to pick up this section of trail right as the Bridge 2 Bridge races were happening. Slalom skiers, inflatable speed boats, jet skis, and other raceable water craft wizzed past us as we meandered along the paved path.

The trail, post river, takes you through Hamilton, and deposits you just west of town at the Taitua Arboretum. The weather was a bit stormy this week, so in true hiker fashion, we hunkered down, with our new British friends, at The Bank for the afternoon. We played cards, drank $4 pints, and enjoyed each other’s company.

Alice and Matt, our fresh favorite British couple.

Feeling fresh, rejuvenated, and healthy, Maya and I set off from the arboretum. Full packs, flexible walking blueprint, and high hopes, met by towering native trees, proved a great start to the next leg of our adventure.

The Karamu Walkway is 8.5 km of rolling hills with cool rocks and sheep. Seriously…sheep EVERYWHERE (25,000 to be exactish, according to our friendly trail host). We are just past the lambing season, so all the mama sheep are sheeping about with their lambs. Very cute, except for the fact that all sheep have a severe case of poopy butt, so just don’t look at their rear.

After our time with the sheep, we experienced our first hut. Picture the AMC’s High Mountain hut system, but a bit smaller, no “Croo”, and the huts are included in our trail pass. Mice…nope. Mattresses…yep. Awesome views and everyone staying there is super friendly…absolutely. The climb up and down the Pirongia Traverse was a true test for Maya’s knee, and she left that stretch feeling tired (of course, it was super muddy!), but energized from how great her legs felt. An overall win, and epic section.

Thank goodness for the board walks as you got closer to the hut.

Sunset with Dr. Seuss tree from the hut deck.

While the sections along the beaches, through farmland, and up and over mountains is why walkers walk, Te Araroa throws some lengthy road walks in there. You know, just to keep you grateful for the time spent not on the road. Walk it, hitch it, whatever. It’s your adventure. Maya and I do put our thumbs out when we can, but if we do end up walking it, we are well prepared with high visibility vests, custom made by Maya herself.

We are currently in Te Kūiti letting some weather pass and planning our next section which includes bike riding and canoe paddling. Sounds like a fun switch up giving our walking legs a rest, and our biking legs/paddling arms, some strength. Looking ahead appears to be pretty dang fun. Stay tuned to find out.

Sources indicate that P.S. I have been carrying a kite, and her maiden voyage was at Putaki Shelter. Her name is Putaki, Taki for short. I tried to fly her again at the Waitomo Top 10 Holiday Park, but the wind had a mind of its own that day. Let’s see how long she last.

Hey there, and welcome (: My name is Gillian. Born and raised in Northern Virginia. Veteran, U.S.C.G. Pinto, if we met on the A.T. in 2023. RPCV Samoa. Always ready for a good laugh. A long walk, to take the edge off. That challenge you did not want, but are grateful for. And a keeper, of the faith, all the love, and this thing called courage (“soft front, strong back”).

📅 03 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (626 w)

Upcoming Route Attempt on Lunag Ri Falls Just Short of Summit

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (626 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Between October 23 and 27, Alexander Parfenov and Alexander Semenov of Russia opened a demanding newly introduced route on 6,895m Lunag Ri in the Rolwaling Himal on the Nepal-Tibet border.
  • The pair climbed a previously unexplored southeast-facing buttress of the Lunag Ri massif.
  • Sources indicate that they placed a piton on the final part of the pillar and began rappelling from there, reaching the base of the wall on October 28, according to gore-ljudje.net.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Between October 23 and 27, Alexander Parfenov and Alexander Semenov of Russia opened a demanding newly introduced route on 6,895m Lunag Ri in the Rolwaling Himal on the Nepal-Tibet border. They turned back short of the summit, which some sources list as 6,907m.

The pair climbed a previously unexplored southeast-facing buttress of the Lunag Ri massif. The line would have ended on the southeast summit. It involved mixed and rock climbing to M6, aid sections of A2–A3, ice up to WI5–WI6 in places, and long stretches of steep snow with limited protection.

Sources indicate that they placed a piton on the final part of the pillar and began rappelling from there, reaching the base of the wall on October 28, according to gore-ljudje.net. The duo turned back short of the summit due to a coming storm and health challenges. The complex summit area — multiple closely linked peaks and ridge features — also left some uncertainty about how close they came to the main summit.

Even without summiting, this was a significant exploration of a major, unclimbed feature on a remote peak.

In a recent development, the upcoming line opened by the Parfenov and Semenov. Photo: Alexander Parfenov.

Lunag Ri, the highest peak in the Lunag massif, has long stood as one of Nepal’s highest unclimbed summits. Early attention focused on the broader massif after Joe Puryear and David Gottlieb made the first ascent of the neighboring 6,778m Jobo Rinjang via its South Face in 2009.

In the same year, a Swiss-led team under Stephane Schaffter attempted lines in the area, including approaches to Lunag I, though their claims about summits on the massif were later met with skepticism in the American Alpine Journal.

Sources indicate that in the autumn of 2010, a French team that included Max Belleville, Mathieu Detrie, Mathieu Maynadier, and Sebastien Ratel climbed the southeast face of Lunag Ri. Their route, Close the Door (1,200 m, IV/5 F5), was completed in a three-day alpine-style push with two bivouacs. They reached a distinct southeast top (6,812m to 6,830m) on the long ridge connecting Lunag I to Jobo Rinjang. By this time, they were exhausted and did not continue the short remaining traverse to the higher main summit. This remains the only major completed route on the Lunag I massif before the first ascent of the true summit.

Industry observers note that from the recent climb on Lunag Ri. Photo: Alexander Parfenov.

Sources indicate that attention then shifted to the west ridge and southwest face of the main peak. In November 2015, Conrad Anker and David Lama’s alpine-style attempt reached a high point roughly 300m below the summit before retreating due to the unexpected complexity of the ridge.

Recent findings suggest that they returned in 2016 to try a similar line. On the first day, at about 5,800m, Anker suffered a heart attack and was evacuated by helicopter. Lama subsequently continued alone on a variation that moved farther right onto an icefield. He established two bivouacs and pushed 50m higher than the previous year’s high point before turning around 250m shy of the summit.

In late October 2018, Lama returned solo. Over three days (October 23-25), with two bivouacs, he climbed the southwest face and northwest/west ridge (1,500m of vertical gain, terrain to 90°). He moved mostly ropeless, with limited self-belaying on the harder mixed sections. Lama negotiated the previously unclimbed headwall and made the final exposed traverse onto the main summit.

Industry observers note that this was the first ascent of Lunag Ri’s highest point. He descended largely by rappelling down the line of ascent. Lama was awarded a Piolet d’Or for this solo first ascent of Lunag Ri.

From the recent climb on Lunag Ri. Photo: Alexander Parfenov.

Floating Alone Down the Brahmaputra on a Bamboo Raft

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (440 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Explorersweb

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Indian mountaineer and adventurer Shekhar Bordoloi has just started a solo expedition down the Brahmaputra River.
  • Recent findings suggest that this won’t be Bordoloi’s first time down the river.
  • Recent findings suggest that bordoloi on a previous raft expedition on the Brahmaputra.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Indian mountaineer and adventurer Shekhar Bordoloi has just started a solo expedition down the Brahmaputra River. He set off on a homemade on a bamboo raft from the Dhola–Sadiya Bridge on November 1 and aims to finish at Dhubri, 891km later. The route covers the entire Brahmaputra within India and should take 22 to 25 days in all. The river begins in Tibet and continues beyond India into Bangladesh, covering 2,900km in all.

Recent findings suggest that this won’t be Bordoloi’s first time down the river. In 2020, he and two friends took a similar bamboo raft down a 400km section of the Brahmaputra. Earlier, in 2015, Bordoloi was one of 11 who tackled another part of the river over 11 days under the auspices of the Assam Mountaineering Association. This expedition, however, will test his endurance, pitting him against river conditions for longer, and with less support, than ever before.

Recent findings suggest that bordoloi on a previous raft expedition on the Brahmaputra. This raft took Bordoloi and friends from the world’s largest river island, Umananda, to its smallest, Majuli. Photo: Shekhar Bordoloi/Instagram.

Industry observers note that bordoloi’s raft was hand-built from bamboo poles carefully lashed together over several days. Such craft are a traditional way of navigating rivers across the region, and are still used by local communities for fishing and transportation.

It has been revealed that though the river can be temperamental, Bordoloi’s first two days have been relatively calm, taking him down the Lohit, one of the Brahmaputra’s many tributaries and channels. Navigating the complex river system alone will be a challenge. The Brahmaputra is one of the largest river systems in India, the ninth-largest in the world by discharge, and is prone to flooding and powerful currents.

Sources indicate that but according to Bordoloi, those obscure, winding corridors are at the heart of this project. Many sections of the river remain underexplored, and he believes there is hidden potential for the people in his home region of Assam. If he can map routes for river tourism and model environmentally responsible river navigation through those routes, he hopes to draw attention to this key riverine ecosystem and the economic opportunities for the people living along it.

It has been revealed that the logistical challenges of a long expedition will further complicate progress. On previous expeditions, Bordoloi traveled with minimal supplies or no food at all, relying entirely on foraging and knowledge of the natural landscape. But this adventure will take over twice as long and may put those skills to their limits.

Bordoloi is documenting his daily progress on Facebook and Instagram.

#33539. Breaking: Te Araroa: more muddy boogeymen

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1230 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Te Araroa: more muddy boogeymen

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1230 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, in order to walk Te Araroa you must accept mud into your heart (and shoes and socks and blisters).
  • I had been thinking about a zero for about a day and a half before that, but had kept pushing on because I wanted to stay with my group.
  • The dome began with fields of mud, and our group split up pretty early into the day.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, in order to walk Te Araroa you must accept mud into your heart (and shoes and socks and blisters). You also must never trust roots for they are deceivers and false friends (slippery, so slippery). The dome is no exception to these rules. You will never escape the mud until you have completed the trail.

Dome day dawned and I was NERVOUS. I had been thinking about a zero for about a day and a half before that, but had kept pushing on because I wanted to stay with my group. I also made the biggest mistake of my life, not having a coffee.

The dome began with fields of mud, and our group split up pretty early into the day. It was the kind of terrain that we all prefer to navigate solo, it’s no fun when people are watching you slip and slide up and down a muddy hill, or you feel like you’re holding others up. I was feeling so rough mentally, and my hiker hunger had really started to kick in the night before, so I spent the morning mentally cataloguing all the food I had left and whether it would be enough to get me to the dairy in Puhoi. I was exhausted physically and mentally before the day even really began. But I kept going.

According to recent reports, when I told people about walking Te Araroa I talked a lot about wanting to build resilience and the ability to keep going even when I really didn’t want to. Some part of me knew this was the first moment where I could start to learn that. So singing broken clips of songs to myself and sometimes even counting my steps, I trudged on.

It has been revealed that I caught up with Sinèad at the end of the first big hill and descent section, and we walked the road section together. I fantasized about going to one of the open houses along the road and asking them for a coffee. I didn’t think they’d let my muddy hiker self in so I kept moving.

When we approached the next big, forested hill section of the day we found a fellow hiker, Xavier, eating half his lunch. I immediately sat down and ate a handful of every one of my accessible snacks. The others took off and I spent a further ten minutes talking myself into continuing. I knew that on the other side of this hill was a campsite where, if I really wanted to, I could stop for the night. I also knew that in less than a kilometre I’d hit the 500km mark.

I felt so sleepy, not just tired but burny-eyes-sleepy. I thought desperately about the single sachet of instant coffee deep in my food bag and sang “just keep swimming” to myself. By the time I was about ¾ through this hill I was once again mentally inventorying my meals, trying to decide if maybe I could break this section into two days.

Then I heard some girls ahead of me and like a puppy seeing its people again after a long work day, I perked up, thinking it was my friends. Unfortunately it was just two very clean-looking, white-sneakered day hikers.

Though they weren’t who I was hoping to see, the whiteness of their sneakers told me that from here, the trail would be more chill. I pushed on and eventually I could hear Sinèad’s accent floating through the trees. And there was our friend, Zoe, getting water from the stream! I crossed the stream and climbed up to the campground where I was delighted to find there was a picnic table so I wouldn’t have to sit on the ground.

In a recent development, I laid out my very wet tent to dry (still thinking about staying there), drank the last of my water, and filtered some into my mayo-turned cold soak jar to shake up my last instant coffee sachet. Sinèad stated she watched me essentially reboot as soon as I started drinking the coffee.

This was when the trail got easier.

It was 1:30 at this point, we’d been walking for six and a half hours, and I didn’t really have a sense of how much further there was to go. I decided to take a long lunch and to eat two wraps, food inventory be damned!

And then my saviours began to arrive. First was another set of day hikers, the older of whom helpfully told me I seemed very tired (I did not hold back when I agreed with him). And then Annabel, who I had been worried about because she normally walks at a similar pace to me and I hadn’t seen her all day.

It has been revealed that after some lecturing about my choice to not wear boots, the day hikers gave me a bag of pumpkin seeds, dates and ANZAC biscuits. The snacks were enough to convince me to put my wet, muddy socks back on and walk the final five or six kilometres to the dome cafe.

Annabel and I climbed the third and final hill of the day which was actually suddenly easy terrain, and then descended a really well-graded, touristy track. I honestly felt like I was flying on that terrain and having Annabel around to chat to made it go really promptly. After eleven hours of walking (including the two hour lunch I took) we made it to camp. The dome cafe was an oasis, it had a bathtub and yes I did sit down in it. I pitched my tent and we all took turns having a hot shower and I think that place saved my life. My mashed potatoes have never tasted better. This was a massive day of learning for me. Mostly that I can do it even when it’s a tough day.

I hope my work colleagues enjoy seeing my muddy sock water.

According to recent reports, anchor me by The Mutton Birds. It should be noted that I did not choose this. It was unceremoniously bestowed upon me by the “here’s a song you didn’t want stuck in your head” gods. But it would be disingenuous to choose anything else because it is what was mostly going through my mind when I wasn’t inventorying my food or dreaming of coffee.

#33538. Breaking: Details, Video of Jugal II First Ascent

📅 04 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (589 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Breaking: Details, Video of Jugal II First Ascent

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (589 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The Spanish team is back in Kathmandu after their first ascent of Jugal II via a highly difficult 2,000m route.
  • The peak, northeast of Kathmandu on the Nepal-Tibet border, has been a coveted goal since it opened to climbing teams in 2023.
  • Route topo, including a special mention of Nives Meroi and Romano Benet.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Spanish team is back in Kathmandu after their first ascent of Jugal II via a highly difficult 2,000m route. Yet, the climbers insist that the best part of the experience was climbing part of the route with Italians Nives Meroi and Romano Benet. Jugal II was Initiative B for the Italian pair after flooding washed out access to their primary target, Tilicho Peak in the Annapurna region.

The peak, northeast of Kathmandu on the Nepal-Tibet border, has been a coveted goal since it opened to climbing teams in 2023. In the end, it was the skill and smart strategy of Mikel Zabalza, Ruben Perez, and Mikel Saez de Urabain that put them on the unclimbed 6,518m summit after an alpine-style push via the east-southeast face.

Route topo, including a special mention of Nives Meroi and Romano Benet.

The team stated that the greatest technical difficulties came high on the route. “From the upper bivouac, the climb goes on pretty vertical mixed terrain, with sections of poor-quality rock,” Zabalza explained. “It’s sustained M5 with some even harder sections, until 6,450m. Then the rest of the way to the summit follows along a 55˚-60˚snow slope.”.

A tough, vertical mixed section. Photo: Mikel Zabalza.

They reached the summit on October 29, at 4:00 pm. The weather was clear but very cold, with some evening humidity.

“We made three bivouacs on the route, two on the way up and one more on descent, and all of them were rather precarious,” Mikel Zabalza told ExplorersWeb from Kathmandu. “Luckily, we had a tarp to enlarge them.”.

According to recent reports, one of the climbers on the summit of Jugal II. Photo: Mikel Zabalza.

The Spanish team, all highly experienced alpinists, had been studying the route for months. This was key to their success.

The situation was different for Benet and Meroi of Italy. Since they had not planned to do Jugal II, their approach to the route was more improvisational. They had no previous information about what they would find. To make matters worse, the third member of the team, Tine Cuder of Slovenia, had to abandon the expedition due to health problems.

One of the Spanish team’s bivouacs, with a tiny ledge enlarged by a fabric tarp. Photo: Romano Benet.

According to recent reports, there was no competition between the two teams, who happily joined forces for the summit push. However, the Spaniards’ strategy proved essential on the highly steep ramps covered with unstable snow.

According to recent reports, nivel Meroi loaded with bivy gear on highly steep mixed ramps on Jugal II. Photo: Romano Benet.

“We set off on an adventure, having never seen the mountain before and not knowing what kind of ascent awaited us, but we gave it a try,” Romano Benet reported from Kathmandu. “We decided to turn back to avoid a third bivouac. ”.

In a recent development, the two teams joined forces and were in good spirits on the route. Photo: Romano Benet.

Benet explained that they lacked the necessary gear (specifically, a tarp like Zabalza’s group) to pitch bivvies “on this type of face, where it’s impossible to carve out a ledge.”.

Otherwise, the two groups returned as friends. “Nives and Romano are exceptional people,” Zabalza remarked.

“We are back from the mountain with new experiences and ideas but, most of all, with three new fantastic friends with whom, hopefully, we will share more adventures in the future,” Romano Benet concluded.

The Spanish team sent us the video below summarizing the climb.

Latest Update: Huge Crowds Trek to Everest Base Camp

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (541 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the image of an endless line of trekkers heading to Everest Base Camp this week seemed like deja vu.
  • Ngima Sherpa of Osprey Adventure explained that this is not the norm, but the delay caused by Cyclone Anwar, which hit Nepal last weekend, has created a huge backlog.
  • Recent findings suggest that “Even though there are always a lot of trekkers heading to Everest Base Camp, this kind of traffic is not usual,” Ngima Sherpa explained.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the image of an endless line of trekkers heading to Everest Base Camp this week seemed like deja vu. Why are conga lines similar to the infamous ones filmed every May on Everest’s Hillary Step, now repeating at the base of the mountain? We asked the local trekking guide who shot the video.

Ngima Sherpa of Osprey Adventure explained that this is not the norm, but the delay caused by Cyclone Anwar, which hit Nepal last weekend, has created a huge backlog.

Recent findings suggest that “Even though there are always a lot of trekkers heading to Everest Base Camp, this kind of traffic is not usual,” Ngima Sherpa explained. “This video was shot on November 1, after three days of continuous snow and rain…During that time, all the trekkers were stuck in Dingboche, which is two trekking stages away from Everest Base Camp.”.

When the weather finally cleared, all those trekkers set off for EBC at the same time, causing heavy traffic on the route from Dingboche to Gorakshep.

According to recent reports, the recent cyclone is also the reason why the surroundings are so heavily covered in snow. Usually, the entire trail to Everest Base Camp is dry.

The fresh snow on Nepal’s peaks is having consequences for those planning to summit trekking peaks. Conditions on otherwise straightforward snow slopes have become problematic, as climbers sink into deep, heavy snow.

Satori Adventures had to retreat after swimming in snow on the flanks of Mera Peak, in the Khumbu. “Four to five feet of fresh snow made it impossible to move forward above high camp,” leader Furba Sherpa reported.

In a recent development, ramesh Gurung noted today that he has retreated from an attempt on 6,119m Lobuche East, another popular Khumbu 6000’er. However, Gurung stated he will try again with another group soon.

Conditions will change only as the snow transforms under the dimming sun and freezes in the approaching winter temperatures.

On Ama Dablam, Sherpa climbers struggled to reopen the route to Camp 1 on Tuesday but managed to complete it. The route above Camp 1 follows a steep, mixed ridge with less accumulated snow. Several teams are now on their summit rotations and expect to top out in the next few days.

In a recent development, tenzing Sherpa of Gokyo Namaste Lodge has shared some useful information for trekkers who blueprint to cross the huge Ngozumpa Glacier between Gokyo and Dragnag. The recent snowfall makes the usual route less safe, and he recommends following local people along an easier route between Longbanga Tso (1st Lake) and Taujung Tso (2nd Lake). See Tenzing’s sketch of the route:.

Alternative route between Gokyo Lakes, suggested by Gokyo Tenzing Sherpa.

Tenzing also noted that the route from Thame to Gokyo is open, as the Gokyo Lodge Association cleared and reopened the trail from the Gokyo side yesterday. However, conditions on the glacier may change quickly.

In a recent development, the route across Gokyo is one of the most popular side trips in the Khumbu, for those wanting to enrich their Everest Base Camp trek. The area features stunning scenery, with high mountain lakes, glaciers, and a view of the formidable South Face of Cho Oyu.

#33535. Latest Update: Animal Attack Roundup, Nov. 4

📅 05 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (939 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Explorersweb ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: Animal Attack Roundup, Nov. 4

📅 05 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (939 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Explorersweb

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that while they predominate the media reports, most animal attack victims are not tourists unwisely attempting to take selfies with wildlife.
  • In a recent development, as expanding populations push human settlements further into wildlife habitat, we can expect to see more conflicts.
  • Photo: Wikimedia Commons/Tisha Mukherjee, CC BY-SA 4.0.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that while they predominate the media reports, most animal attack victims are not tourists unwisely attempting to take selfies with wildlife. People who live and work every day among animals are the ones who most often face the consequences.

In a recent development, as expanding populations push human settlements further into wildlife habitat, we can expect to see more conflicts. Here are some recent incidents.

Photo: Wikimedia Commons/Tisha Mukherjee, CC BY-SA 4.0.

In Indonesia, 24-year-old Selviana Ambu Kaka was attacked by a crocodile while washing clothes in the Bondo Kodi River. Her fiancé and his sister witnessed a large crocodile emerging from the water, biting Ambu Kaka on the leg, and dragging her into the river. They immediately alerted nearby relatives and authorities, and a search commenced.

The people of Southwest Sumba, the closest town, organized and combed the area with nets. When they found a large crocodile matching witness descriptions, they hauled it onto shore and killed it. The animal measured nearly 4.9 meters long.

In a recent development, early on the morning of October 24, Ambu Kaka’s remains were found approximately 30m from the attack site. She is one of many such victims in Indonesia, which sees more saltwater crocodile attacks than any other country.

Habitat destruction is largely behind the massive number of human-crocodile conflicts. It’s an understandably hard sell, however, for conservation workers to convince locals that preventing attacks means protecting the perpetrators.

The victim had recently returned from Jakarta to become formally engaged on October 30.

Photo: Wikimedia Commons/ Rohit Gangwal, CC BY-SA 4.0.

A 65-year-old farm laborer, Tulsi Rama Sawar, was killed by a leopard in state of Maharashtra, just north of Mumbai, on November 1. The noise of the attack summoned help from the locals. By the time they arrived, the leopard had fled, but Sawar was deceased. Her case comes less than a month after a leopard killed a 52-year-old woman in the same area.

Industry observers note that town residents are demanding immediate government action to capture the animal. If their demands for cage traps and cameras are not granted, locals threaten collective protest. The attacks represent a threat to their lives, but also their livelihoods, as farmers are unable to work the fields out of fear of attack.

Recent findings suggest that elsewhere, in Uttar Pradesh near the Nepal border, a 45-year-old farmer named Kennu fought off an attacking leopard, sustaining serious injuries. The man was working in a sugarcane field when the predator leaped out from hiding. Kennu fought back, and the animal retreated long enough for him to flee home, where family members brought him to medical care. Forestry officials have urged agricultural workers to avoid working in the fields alone.

Farm workers are not the only leopard victims, however. Early in the morning of November 4, a 15-year-old girl was dragged from her home in the Shahdol district of central India.

Recent findings suggest that saraswati Singh Gond was sleeping in bed beside her sister on their veranda, which did not have a door. A leopard entered during the night, not even waking her sister. Singh Gond’s body was found approximately 300m from the house. The search for the leopard continues.

Photo: Wikimedia Commons/Shadow Ayush, CC BY-SA 4.0.

In a recent development, leopards are only one of the wildlife threats that rural Indians face. A 55-year-old woman was gathering mushrooms in Utterakand in northern India on October 30 when she was attacked and killed by a wild elephant. Devaki Rana was lifted up and thrown to the ground, her son reported.

The incident occurred in one of India’s elephant corridors, which allow highly endangered Asian elephant herds to move between their fragmented habitats. The corridors are essential to conservation, but also present a concentrated area where attacks are more common.

It has been revealed that another fatal encounter took place in the state of Chhattisgarh in east-central India. A man of between 35 and 40 years of age, traveling by motorcycle with his nephew, came upon an elephant standing in the road. It immediately charged them, killing the uncle, while his nephew managed to hide beneath a parked truck. Eventually, the elephant left, and he was able to escape.

According to recent reports, locals believe that the elephant in question is one known as Kabra Kaan, which they see frequently and which has been connected with earlier incidents. The Forestry Department, however, has not confirmed this.

Recent findings suggest that elephant corridors allow them to pass between the remaining forested areas. Photo: Wildlife Trust of India.

Recent findings suggest that in Japan, brown bear attacks have been rising for several years. As in many places, human settlements are encroaching on brown bear territory. A decrease in farmland has left no boundary between the urban and the forested worlds. The government has responded with controversial bear culls, despite the concerns of conservation workers.

The latest incident is very different from the increasingly common attack stories. Late on the night of October 30, an express train running on Hokkaido’s Soya Line collided with a large brown bear. The body of the bear was trapped under the train, and the wheels derailed.

A brown bear became trapped beneath the wheels of Sarobetsu No 3. Photo: Hokkaido Railway Firm.

Sources indicate that none of the crew or 32 passengers were injured in the crash. However, fearing more bears were in the area, officials kept everyone on the train overnight, until they could be safely extracted the following morning. Firm officials have confirmed that this is the first bear-collision derailment in their nearly 40-year history.

#33534. Yosemite At Last! — John Muir Trail Day 21

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 13m • 📚 Deep Dive (2603 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Yosemite At Last! — John Muir Trail Day 21

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2603 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that it was a fitful, fretful night.
  • On one of those, in the middle of the night, I did something clever.
  • Above all, I worried about what I would be facing in the morning.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Total Elevation Gain:  46,975 feet.

Pace (minutes per mile):  28:21.

It has been revealed that it was a fitful, fretful night. It continued to rain for a while, off and on, and the wind came up again, continuing throughout the night. The whole time I was worrying about staying warm, staying dry, and making the fewest possible excursions outside to pee.

On one of those, in the middle of the night, I did something clever. I picked up my poncho, which was just lying on the ground soaking wet, and I draped it over a pine tree, so it looked like a scarecrow. Or maybe a scare-bear?

Above all, I worried about what I would be facing in the morning.

Indeed, the morning came. I got up reasonably early, at 6:30, and had breakfast in my tent. In my warm, now semi-dry tent.

The good thing was that the rain had stopped. The poncho I stood up as a decoy in the night, was now wind dried. So, I used it for staging. I put it on the wet ground and pulled all of my stuff out of the tent and placed it on the dry poncho. If things were dry, they stayed dry; if wet, at least they didn’t get any wetter.

Things looked a LOT better at my camp site in the morning!

Industry observers note that this mattered, because I had a lot of wet stuff. I had a wet hoodie. I had wet shorts, wet socks, and wet shoes.

After evacuating the tent, I took it down. Thanks to the wind, the fly – that had been soaking wet — was basically dry. But the ground cloth and the bottom of the tent were very wet.

What to do? I could either dry them and be done with it, or pack them wet, and dry them later. While thinking about this, I put them on logs, and laid them out to dry, so that my indecision became a decision. When the sun peeked out a little, I put them on rocks. Yes, it ate up a lot of time, but when they were finally dry, I could stop worrying about that issue and just hike.

According to recent reports, at 9:00 a.m. I set off. I was wearing wet-cold shoes, wet-cold shorts, wet-cold gloves, a wet-cold hoodie, and a wet-cold hat. Only one thing was not wet and cold:  I decided to go ahead and use my dry socks. I hoped that my shoes were just moist and not soaking wet, and my dry socks would be a barrier to that moisture. That strategy worked out pretty well.

It has been revealed that because it was cold in the aftermath of the storm, I started with a lot of energy, to get my blood flowing. I needed it too, for the trail sang one refrain:  up, up, up, and up.

Looking back at the hill I climbed — but at least I was warm, and getting dry!

Sources indicate that by the time I reached the ridge, and looked down on Garnet Lake, I was mostly dry and all warmed up. Then I got lost.

I could see Garnet Lake, I just couldn’t see how to GET there!

Recent findings suggest that I knew I had to go east, and I spotted a little trail to the east, so I started down that trail until it kind of disappeared. Then I spent about ten minutes wandering around up there, trying to find my way, unable to believe the east-going trail was a false trail. Finally, I retraced my steps far enough to notice a separate west-going trail. That was counterintuitive, but it was the correct trail, because it eventually looped around, lower down, and went east, as I knew it should.

I name this “One Pine Tree Island” in Garnet Lake.

Walking along the shore of Garnet Lake I envisioned what might have happened if I had made it to this destination in the storm the day before. I could imagine myself, struggling with my tent in the rain, and having a huge gust of wind lift the tent like a beach ball and deposit it in the middle of the lake! It would have been bad! Yes, hilarious, but bad.

To reinforce the power of the storm the day before, this was Ninja Queen’s  description of her experience, as she sent it to me via text, with almost no editing:.

Industry observers note that “…you can imagine how horribly wrong the day of the storm went for me. I should have hunkered down early like most other hikers had, but I foolishly trusted my (Garmin) InReach weather forecast a little too much, went over Island Pass (a tiny pass but a pass nonetheless) when the storm hit full force two hours early. It was bad. Really, really bad. The trail flooded very rapidly, got washed out and started diverging in multiple directions from the torrential downpour. They were ankle-deep and I kept losing the actual trail; it had become mini rivers at that point. Needless to say, I got wetted out through and through, shivering intensely, my hands no longer functioning, unable to take another step. I ended up setting up camp on some random flat-ish spot over some vegetation that also started pooling water. I was so afraid my tent was going to get flooded. Almost everything inside the tent was wet and muddy as well, though I was able to change into dry sleep clothes and sleeping bag, thanks to my nylofume pack liners. It took me a couple of hours, but I eventually warmed up in the bag, cooked and ate food inside (bears were the last of my worries at this point) and drank as little water as possible so I wouldn’t have to go out until the next morning. Putting back on cold, dripping wet clothes the next morning felt torture-adjacent; something I hope I’ll never have to go through again.”.

“It gave me a small chuckle seeing other hikers also emerge from non-established tent sites the next morning. I quickly learned what I went through was not a typical rainstorm experience. Almost everyone I talked to stated it had been one of the worst storms they’ve seen on trail. One guy, a firefighter, told me this was far worse than the hurricane weather he had caught on the AT (Appalachian Trail) a few years back. Now I felt like a survivor, instead of feeling like a fair weather backpacker who crumbled at the slightest hint of bad weather.”.

In a recent development, I filled up my water at the bridge where a stream exits the lake. There were a lot of folks around there, laying out their tents to dry from the storm. It was surprising, and a little disturbing, to see how much foam, and even spume-like foam, was on Garnet Lake, which looks otherwise pristine. I didn’t ask anybody about it at the time, who would I ask?

But later I Googled AI and discovered:  “…foam usually forms naturally when decaying plants, algae, and organic debris release compounds that lower water surface tension, and wind or wave action whips air into bubbles.”  In other words, the wind from the storm had produced the foam, not some giant industrial complex just out of view!

According to recent reports, I continued up, from Garnet to beautiful Ruby Lake, then to Emerald Lake, and finally the Thousand Islands Lake. This was an exceptionally scenic stretch.

I think this was Ruby Lake… if the water were sparkling red, it would be easier to tell!

Of course this was Thousand Islands Lake — with a pretty terrific backdrop!

It has been revealed that there was very little elevation gain from there to Island Pass. Once the trail reached the ridge on the opposite side of the lake it seemed to stay at a mostly constant elevation for a very long time. The longer it went on, the more I wondered, “Pass? Is there really a pass up here somewhere? Where?”.

No pass, but a pretty cool-looking mushroom!

How can you tell when you have reached a pass? When you can see the other side of the mountain. It felt like that was never going to happen.

Sources indicate that finally, it was getting to be lunchtime. I decided to sit next to a charming little pond up there, and to eat my lunch.

Basically, I ate half of the food that I had brought as lunch, saving the other half for “second lunch.”  But afterwards, I just didn’t feel like I had much energy. Even finally reaching the edge did not inspire me. I saw the edge of the pass and started heading down, but my legs felt heavy. My legs felt like limp spaghetti.

Sources indicate that when your legs don’t want to go, you need your brain to execute an override. So, I forced myself to keep going. Finally, I stopped again and made myself a second lunch in that sort of halfway space between Island Pass and Donohue Pass. About five miles separated them and Donohue represented the entrance to Yosemite National Park.

A dead tree by a stream; dead is how I felt before second lunch!

After lunch I had more energy, and I continued.

Throughout the JMT, whenever I approached a location where I knew there was a pass in the ridgeline, I always looked up to see if I could figure out where it might be. “Is that it? No, is that it? Wait, is that it?”  I suspect most hikers do this.

With Donohue Pass it was hidden around the corner of an extending hump of rock, so of course I guessed wrong. Just short of the summit, I saw a full backpack about 25 yards from the trail. That seemed strange and I looked around. Was someone off going to the bathroom? There was nothing but silence. I continued on, but with a nagging worry for whoever was not connected with their pack.

When I arrived on top, at 11,066 feet elevation, I was all alone. In honor of my son Gabriel, who coined the pun, I bellowed, “YO! SEMITE!!!”  I got no answer, not even an echo. Even so, I was in Yosemite. It felt strange to be just a few days from the end — barring injury, of course.

As I headed down from Donohue, I thought, “On the one hand, I don’t want to set up in the dark. But there are not too many campsites up here and, of course, I am a couple of miles behind schedule because of the storm.”  I resolved to take a chance and push it a little bit.

As a result, the riverside campsites just below Donohue Pass did not tempt me; they were filling up in any case.

The first camp north of Donohue Pass was by this ugly little lake….

It has been revealed that instead, I descended rapidly and with determination. As I did, I encountered a group heading southbound, up to the pass behind me. One young man was not carrying a pack. Apparently, he had come down to assist his family in making the ascent. He told me, “I left my pack up near the Pass so that I would not be encumbered in helping my family.”  I breathed deeply; mystery solved.

Industry observers note that the first stretch went through rocky scree. I asked the mountain gods, “Why is there so much rocky scree?”  They rewarded me with forest.

See the meadow, far below there? My campsite was somewhere down there….

Industry observers note that the descent continued sharply through the woods, and I passed several gorgeous camping sites near the steeply dropping steam. Each time I told myself, “No! Not yet!” and then each time I regretted it, and wondered if I would ever find another spot, after that perfect one I had just rejected.

According to recent reports, at last, the steep downhill tapered off, and I reached the valley at the bottom. The stream, now wider and larger, and the trail continued to parallel each other. The going became easier for both the water and my legs.

Industry observers note that following the river there were a few more possible places. As the sun slipped behind the mountains, but still with plenty of light, I saw a knoll overlooking a wide meadow. On that knoll was a lovely camping spot. I was home for the night.

The sun remains on the hillside, even as it gets dark in the valley.

My dinner was rice and beans and chicken, Santa Fe style. I let it soak as I pitched my tent and arranged my site. I let it soak some more as I explored higher up, in the giant granite boulders above the site, to find a cat hole location. It soaked still longer as I dug the hole in preparation for the next morning. But then, with no chores left to do, I got impatient. I ate.

Industry observers note that the dish was very well-seasoned, very tasty. This was certainly a meal I would recommend having again, on another hike, in another place. But rice takes a long time to absorb water when cold-soaking, and I didn’t wait long enough. The flavors were great, but the rice was… crunchy. I didn’t care much. It had been a strenuous day, coming the day after the intense storm. I was tired and hungry and starved for calories. I ate it all with gusto, crunch and all!

I was feeling good. It was a long day, and I had crossed two passes. I was finally in Yosemite. I haven’t mentioned the aftermath of my fall too much in recent posts, but my ribs were finally hurting less. My wrist was still a problem, to some degree, but it was functional.

The next day, I would be passing through Tuolumne Meadow. There I would either get a permit for Half Dome, or I would not. If I did, I probably had three days of hiking left. If I did not, then it would likely be two days. I had well under forty miles to go.

As the twilight deepened, I was loving my campsite facing the open meadow. I was proud of the mileage I had achieved, after the shortened day in the storm. My eyes closed and I welcomed blissful sleep.

#33533. Tech Report: The Long Rainy Road

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1259 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Thetrek ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: The Long Rainy Road

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1259 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Thetrek

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that I have had extraordinary luck to largely avoid precipitation for many weeks.
  • Industry observers note that any hope of escaping with a dry tent vanished in the early morning hours.
  • Industry observers note that A little drizzle began to fall intermittently as I made my way along the rocky trail back to Pulpit Rock.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that I have had extraordinary luck to largely avoid precipitation for many weeks. That is about to change.

Industry observers note that any hope of escaping with a dry tent vanished in the early morning hours. The first domino to fall. Now I had to hope that it wouldn’t be actively raining when it comes time to pack up camp. It quickly becomes impossible to keep my pack dry in such a scenario, how do I keep the pack dry when I have to disassemble and roll up my only dry place? Lucky for me, when light first broke the rain noise had stopped. I patted the walls of my tent to dispel some of the leftover water and checked the time. 6:17AM. I decided to save breakfast for later and go straight into packing up so I could check the sunrise and then get to hiking before the precipitation inevitably arrived. At The Pinnacle my instincts were correct, nothing but a small patch of orange glow that could have been a candy wrapper blowing in the wind. I was unbothered, any day where there is rain but I don’t have to pack up in the rain is alright with me. With rain imminent I chose to throw on my poncho, though that decision was partially based on the chillier than expected morning and early start time.

Industry observers note that A little drizzle began to fall intermittently as I made my way along the rocky trail back to Pulpit Rock. Conveniently, I can save a few rocky steps by taking the clear driveway past the the Lehigh Valley Amateur Astronomical Society observatories. Its worth mentioning that the society provides a privy and trash can that can be used by hikers. They do ask that hikers don’t camp on the property or use flashlights, for obvious reasons. At the far end of the site I arrived at Pulpit Rock, which still offered a nice view despite the cloudy skies.

From there I didn’t hesitate to use the road down from the observatories all the way down to the Windsor Furnace Shelter. I had a quick breakfast and got back on trail before 8:30AM. Hardly any rain had fallen, I wondered if I’d again be getting lucky with the weather and get all the way back to my van without getting soaked. I pushed hard to get the 5 or so miles to Port Clinton done. I knew the steep leafy trail awaited me and I was holding my breathe to get through that section before any heavy rain arrived – it would not be fun going up that section if the trail was steep, leafy, and turning into a stream all at the same time.

Sources indicate that remarkably, the rain continued to hold off. I got closer and closer to Port Clinton, slowly realizing that the 60% chance of rain I saw for nearly every hour the day was landing in the 40% zone at least to start the day. I made it down the trail into town, back across the Schuykill River, and through the train yard. I charged up the hill, still expecting rain at any moment. The climb up proved tough, but not as treacherous as the climb down. This is the one time working against gravity actually works with you. Soon I was back on the ridge and heading toward the gravel road that would take me all the way back to my van on route 183. I thought that if the rain fell there it wouldn’t be a big deal, the hiking would at least be easy.

The Lehigh Valley Amateur Astronomical Society observatories near Pulpit Rock.

Breakfast at the Windsor Furnace Shelter.

A steep climb coming out of the Windsor Furnace Shelter.

In a recent development, I was just starting to think of the impossible. Could I get all the way back to my van without any serious rain? It would take about 3 and half hours to get all the way back to my van hiking at full bore on the gravel road. I didn’t have any stops to make, I was in a straight race with nature. My hopes slowly grew and then, with a single sound, were completely erased. On a downhill section of the road I heard thunder ahead. The forecast didn’t say anything about thunderstorms, but I suppose it didn’t say it would be dry for the better part of the morning either. I was fairly exposed on the road, there was going to be rain, and soon it came. I pulled my poncho back over me, I had stashed it over my shoulders during the climb to stay cool, staying dry was the priority now.

The wind blew and the rain progressed rapidly from light drizzle to a steady downpour. The thunder bellowed louder and I began seeing flashes of lightning. The the rain started to feel sharp on my exposed hands. My gloves aren’t waterproof so it isn’t really worth it wear them in the rain. The rain had become freezing rain. Then it became hail the size of Nerds candy. The hail only lasted a few minutes, but the rain continued on. Although the day was in the mid 40s, the rain was ice cold. As soon as the rain became heavy my shoes and socks flooded. All I could do was shake my head and laugh, I had finally run out of luck, and things were regressing to the mean, emphasis on mean.

In a recent development, none of the surprisingly severe weather slowed me down. I was determined to get back to my van and get dry. The rain continued for almost 2 hours. When it did finally stop, I noticed that the water drops on the trees appeared frozen in place. It looked like ice hanging on the branches and made it look a lot like I was hiking on a rainy, cold winter afternoon. For good, measure, the sun decided to come out with about 30 minutes left. A nice thought, but it was going to take more than a few rays of sunlight to dry out my shoes.

Walking the gravel road just before the weather arrived.

Walking the gravel road just before the weather arrived.

It’s hard to see in the picture, but the scene had gotten considerably more wintery.

Near the end of the hike, the sun comes out.

Total: 24.4 miles, 45,270 steps.
